title: Project Structure - Monorepo vs Separate Repos
context:
You specified:
- Backend: Java 21 + Spring Boot 4 + SQLite
- Frontend: React 18 + MUI

These are two different technology stacks that will need to communicate.
ambiguity: It's unclear whether this should be organized as a monorepo (single repository with /backend and /frontend folders) or as separate repositories for backend and frontend.
question: How should the project structure be organized?

options.label: Monorepo (Recommended)
options.description: Single repository with /backend and /frontend folders. Easier coordination, shared versioning, simpler deployment setup.

options.label: Separate repositories
options.description: Independent repos for backend and frontend. More flexibility for independent deployment and scaling, but requires API versioning strategy.

title: API Architecture and Communication Pattern
context:
The application needs:
- File viewing (CBR/CBZ extraction and serving)
- Position tracking
- Rating system
- TTS processing with LLM integration
- Admin functionality (user/file management, logs)

This involves multiple API endpoints with different characteristics (file streaming, metadata CRUD, async processing).
ambiguity: The API design pattern isn't specified. Different patterns suit different use cases.
question: Which API architecture should be used for frontend-backend communication?

options.label: RESTful API (Recommended)
options.description: Standard REST endpoints. Best for file serving, CRUD operations, well-documented Spring Boot support. Straightforward for admin panel.

options.label: GraphQL API
options.description: Single endpoint with flexible queries. Good for complex data fetching, but adds complexity and may be overkill for this use case.

options.label: Hybrid (REST + WebSockets)
options.description: REST for CRUD/files, WebSockets for real-time TTS processing status updates. More complex but provides live progress feedback.

title: Database Schema for File Metadata and Processing Results
context:
You mentioned:
- SQLite for storage
- Files stored on disk
- Need to track: positions, ratings, TTS processing results (JSON with speakers/audio)
- User management, audit logs

TTS results could be large JSON objects with page-by-page speaker identification and audio file references.
ambiguity: How should TTS processing results and file metadata be stored in the database? Large JSON objects in SQLite can impact performance.
question: How should TTS processing results and complex metadata be stored?

options.label: JSON columns in SQLite (Recommended)
options.description: Store TTS results as JSON in the database. Simple, everything in one place, SQLite supports JSON functions since 3.38.0. Good for moderate file sizes.

options.label: Separate JSON files on disk
options.description: Store TTS results as .json files alongside the CBR/CBZ files. Database only stores file paths. Better for very large results, requires file management.

options.label: Normalized relational tables
options.description: Create tables: Pages, Speakers, AudioSegments with foreign keys. More complex schema but better queryability and data integrity.

title: CBR/CBZ File Processing Strategy
context:
CBR/CBZ files are comic book archives:
- CBZ = ZIP archive with images
- CBR = RAR archive with images

The viewer needs to:
- Extract individual pages
- Serve them to frontend
- Support both fullscreen and scrolling modes

This can be done on-the-fly or pre-processed.
ambiguity: Should files be extracted on-the-fly when viewing, or pre-extracted when uploaded?
question: How should CBR/CBZ files be processed for viewing?

options.label: On-the-fly extraction (Recommended)
options.description: Extract pages from archive when requested. Saves disk space, no preprocessing delay. May need caching for performance.

options.label: Pre-extract on upload
options.description: Extract all pages when file is uploaded. Faster viewing, but uses more disk space. Easier to implement image optimization.

options.label: Hybrid with caching
options.description: Extract on-demand, cache extracted pages in temporary storage. Balance between disk space and performance.

title: TTS Processing Workflow and User Experience
context:
You specified TTS processing should:
1. Be on-demand (user requests it)
2. Use LLM for OCR (OpenAI API + Claude API)
3. Prepare JSON with speakers
4. Use Minimax API for TTS
5. Store results with files

This is a multi-step async process that could take several minutes for a full comic book.
ambiguity: How should the TTS processing workflow be presented to the user? Should they wait, or can they navigate away?
question: How should TTS processing be handled from a user experience perspective?

options.label: Async with progress tracking (Recommended)
options.description: User requests TTS, gets a job ID, can navigate away. Progress shown via polling or WebSocket. Notified when complete. Best UX for long processes.

options.label: Synchronous blocking
options.description: User waits on the page until processing completes. Simple to implement but poor UX for long waits. Risk of timeout.

options.label: Background queue system
options.description: User requests TTS, it's queued for background processing. No progress tracking, user checks back later. Simplest backend, minimal UX feedback.

title: Authentication and Authorization Strategy
context:
You mentioned:
- User management in admin panel
- File viewing (presumably users need accounts)
- Admin vs regular user roles implied

Spring Boot 4 supports multiple auth strategies.
ambiguity: What authentication mechanism should be implemented? This affects both backend and frontend architecture.
question: Which authentication strategy should be used?

options.label: JWT tokens (Recommended)
options.description: Stateless authentication, tokens stored in frontend (localStorage/sessionStorage). Standard for React SPAs, good for REST APIs. Requires token refresh strategy.

options.label: Session-based (cookies)
options.description: Server-side sessions with HTTP-only cookies. More secure against XSS, but requires session storage. Traditional approach.

options.label: OAuth2 / SSO
options.description: External authentication provider (Google, GitHub, etc.). More complex but professional. Good if you want social login.

title: File Storage and Serving Strategy
context:
You specified:
- Files stored on disk (first approach)
- Backend serves files to frontend
- Need to serve individual pages from CBR/CBZ archives
- Need to serve generated audio files

File serving can be handled by Spring Boot directly or delegated to a web server.
ambiguity: How should static files (comic pages, audio) be served to the frontend?
question: What's the file serving strategy?

options.label: Spring Boot serves everything (Recommended for MVP)
options.description: Spring Boot handles all file serving via controllers. Simple, everything in one place. May need optimization later for high traffic.

options.label: Nginx/Apache reverse proxy
options.description: Web server in front serves static files, proxies API calls to Spring Boot. Better performance, more production-ready, but more complex setup.

options.label: CDN for files
options.description: Files served from CDN (S3 + CloudFront, etc.). Best performance, higher cost, requires file upload to cloud. Overkill for 'hosted somewhere' MVP.

title: Frontend State Management Approach
context:
The React frontend needs to manage:
- Current file and page position
- User preferences (fullscreen vs scroll mode)
- TTS processing status
- Admin panel data (users, files, logs)
- Authentication state

React 18 supports various state management approaches.
ambiguity: What state management strategy should the React frontend use?
question: Which state management approach for the React frontend?

options.label: React Context + Hooks (Recommended)
options.description: Built-in React features, no external dependencies. Good for moderate complexity. Use Context for global state (auth, current file), hooks for local state.

options.label: Redux Toolkit
options.description: Centralized state management with Redux. Better for complex state logic, time-travel debugging. More boilerplate, may be overkill.

options.label: Zustand or Jotai
options.description: Lightweight state management libraries. Less boilerplate than Redux, more structure than Context. Modern, simple API.

options.label: React Query + Context
options.description: React Query for server state (API data, caching), Context for client state (UI preferences). Separation of concerns, excellent caching.

title: Testing Approach for Full-Stack Application
context:
This is a greenfield project with:
- Backend: Spring Boot 4 (supports JUnit 5, MockMvc, TestContainers)
- Frontend: React 18 (supports Jest, React Testing Library, Cypress, Playwright)
- Integration points: File processing, LLM APIs, TTS generation

Testing strategy affects project structure and CI/CD setup.
ambiguity: What level of testing should be implemented from the start?
question: What testing strategy should be established?

options.label: Unit + Integration tests (Recommended)
options.description: Backend: JUnit for services, MockMvc for controllers. Frontend: Jest + React Testing Library for components. No E2E initially. Practical balance.

options.label: Full testing pyramid
options.description: Unit + Integration + E2E (Playwright/Cypress). Most comprehensive, but slower to implement and run. Best for production-critical apps.

options.label: Minimal testing
options.description: Only critical path tests. Faster initial development, but risky for refactoring. Add tests incrementally as issues arise.

title: LLM Integration for OCR - Provider Strategy
context:
You specified:
- OpenAI API + Claude API for OCR
- Need to extract text and identify speakers from comic pages
- Results stored as JSON

Using multiple LLM providers requires a strategy.
ambiguity: How should the dual LLM provider setup work? Should both be used, or is one a fallback?
question: What's the strategy for using OpenAI + Claude for OCR?

options.label: Primary + Fallback
options.description: Try OpenAI first, fall back to Claude if it fails or hits rate limits. Resilient, but requires error handling and retry logic.

options.label: User/Admin configurable
options.description: Admin chooses which provider to use in settings. Simple, flexible, allows testing both. User or admin can switch based on cost/quality.

options.label: Both used for validation
options.description: Send to both APIs, compare results for accuracy. Best quality, but 2x cost and slower. Overkill unless quality is critical.

options.label: Load balancing
options.description: Distribute requests across both providers to avoid rate limits. Complex, requires request tracking. Good for high volume.

title: User Position Tracking Granularity
context:
You mentioned the app should 'remember positions of the files'.

This could mean:
- Last page viewed in each comic
- Scroll position within a page (for scroll mode)
- Reading history with timestamps
- Multiple bookmarks per file
ambiguity: What level of detail should position tracking store?
question: How detailed should position tracking be?

options.label: Last page only (Recommended)
options.description: Store one 'current page' number per file per user. Simple, covers the core use case. User resumes where they left off.

options.label: Page + scroll position
options.description: Store page number and Y-scroll position for scroll mode. More precise, especially for long vertical pages. Slightly more complex.

options.label: Full reading history
options.description: Track every page view with timestamps. Enables analytics (reading speed, re-reads). Good for 'continue reading' + statistics.

options.label: Multiple bookmarks
options.description: Users can save multiple positions per file. Like browser bookmarks. More features, more UI complexity.

title: Deployment Environment and Hosting
context:
You mentioned the app 'will be hosted somewhere'.

This affects:
- Build process and packaging
- Database path configuration (SQLite file location)
- File storage paths
- Environment variable management
- CORS configuration
question: Where and how will this application be deployed?

options.label: Single server (VM/VPS)
options.description: Deploy both frontend and backend on one server. Frontend built and served by Spring Boot or Nginx. Simple, traditional approach. Good for MVP.

options.label: Docker containers
options.description: Containerized backend + frontend. Can run on any container platform (Docker Compose, Kubernetes, cloud). Portable, reproducible.

options.label: Separate hosting
options.description: Frontend on Vercel/Netlify, backend on Heroku/Railway/cloud VM. Easier CI/CD, but requires CORS setup and more configuration.

options.label: Cloud platform (AWS/GCP/Azure)
options.description: Full cloud deployment with managed services. Scalable, professional, but more complex and potentially costly. Overkill for MVP.
